See Barrett v. Berryhill, 906 F.3d 340 (Sth Cir. 2018); Passmore v. Astrue, 533

3. THE PRESIDING OFFICIAL
Perhaps the most important component of formq 1 adjudicatory 
procedure involves the official responsible for presiding over the hAaring 
Determining this official s position and powers is a matter of procedural 
design that necessarily implicates constitutional concerns and intertwines 
with the challenges of sound administration.
a. Neutrality and Statutory Separation of Functions
That the persons who constitute an agency—SEC Commissioners (as 
in SEC V. Jarkesy, supra), NLRB Board Members, the FDA Commissioner, 
or the Secretary of Transportation—may be ultimately responsible for 
investigation, prosecution, and final decision making in the same case is a 
well-entrenched feature of American ad m i n i str gti ye law. Such 
combinations of functions inspired intense opposition to a dministmtiv a  
regulation in the New Deal era and in the years leading up to the adoption 
of the APA in 1946. Administrative agencies were chastised as “that hybrid 
thing beloved by tyrants and abhorred by free men,” and the ABA Special 
Comniittee on Administrative Law in 1934 strongly argued that the 
adjudicatory functions of agencies be transferred to an a  dministrative 
court or courts. Partisans on the other side inflamed the debate by 
advocating that independent regulatory commissions be absorbed into the 
executive branch to make them more responsive to governmAnf.a  1 policy. 
See generally ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURE IN GOVERNMENT AGENCIES vi 
(Charles K. Woltz ed., 1968).
The general approach to separation of functions that has prevailed at 
the federal level, however, is that recommended by the Attorney General’s 
Committee on Administrative Procedure and embodied in the APA—an 
internal separation of personnel within agencies for purposes of formal 
adjudication, which results in clear divisions of responsibility at the lower 
levels of adjudication and an insulation of even top administrators from 
investigative and prosecutorial staff, save on the public record.
